The part that made me mad wasn’t that she almost hit us. It was what my insurance company said two weeks later. I was driving with my wife and kids in the car, doing 29 in a 30, when this woman came flying up behind us like we were personally ruining her day. She got so close I couldn’t even see her headlights anymore. My wife looked in the side mirror and said, “What is she doing?” I said, “Trying to climb into the trunk, apparently.” I put my turn signal on early because we were turning in about half a block. That somehow made her angrier. She came even closer, threw her hands up, and nearly followed us through the turn like she was going to push us into it. We pulled into the parking lot. I thought she’d keep going. She didn’t. She pulled in behind us, jumped out, and started yelling before I even opened my door. My kids were quiet in the back seat. My wife was telling me not to get out. This woman was shouting because I had the nerve to drive the speed limit. That was the whole crime. Driving the speed limit with my family in the car. Eventually she got back in her car and sped off like she hadn’t just almost caused two accidents in three minutes. Nobody got hurt. But I sat there for a second thinking, this is why normal people pay more. Because there are drivers out there treating every road like they’re late for a court date. Two weeks later, my renewal email came in. $318 a month. For our two cars. I thought it had to be a mistake. I’ve got a clean record. No major accidents. No DUI. I don’t drive like an idiot. My wife drives the same route every day. Most weeks my car is either in the driveway, at the grocery store, or parked at my kid’s practice. So I called. The rep was nice. That somehow made it more annoying. She said our rate changed because of updated risk in our area. I asked her what that meant. She said accident frequency, claims volume, uninsured drivers, repair costs, and other local rating factors. I said, “So my zip code has a bad driving record?” She paused. Then she said, “That’s not exactly how we phrase it.” But that was exactly what it was. I wasn’t being priced like me. I was being priced like every aggressive, uninsured, distracted, bumper-riding driver around me. The woman who almost hit my family was gone. But somehow she was still on my bill. I told the rep I hadn’t caused any claims. She said she understood. I told her I’d been with them for years. She said she understood. I told her I was not interested in paying more because other people can’t act normal behind the wheel. She said she understood. The bill did not understand. After I hung up, I complained about it for probably twenty minutes. My wife finally said, “Then check somewhere else.” I told her I didn’t want to spend the whole night calling insurance companies. She said, “I didn’t say call. I said check.” Fair. So I opened my laptop and started looking. Most of it was exactly what I expected. Pages that wanted too much information. Sites that looked like they were built to sell my phone number. Forms that felt like a trap. Then I found one that was simple. It checked real rates from companies competing for the same driver at the same time. Same cars. Same address. Same coverage levels. Same driving record. No credit card. No canceling anything first. No waiting for an agent to call me and ask the same questions again. I figured I had nothing to lose except another few minutes. So I entered the info. The rate came back at $97 a month. For both cars. Same liability limits. Same comprehensive and collision. Same deductible. I just stared at it. Not because $97 was cheap. Because $318 suddenly looked ridiculous. My wife walked by and asked, “Did you find anything?” I turned the laptop toward her. She looked at the screen and said, “That’s for both cars?” I said yes. She said, “And we’re paying three hundred eighteen?” I said yes. She said, “Switch it.” That was it. No big debate. No loyalty speech. No waiting around. No second-guessing. We had a lower option with the same coverage, so we took it. We switched. The weirdest part was how normal it felt afterward. Same cars in the same driveway. Same drivers. Same clean record. Same errands, same school runs, same grocery store, same roads. The only thing that changed was we stopped letting one company decide what our risk was worth. That was 4 months ago. We’ve saved almost $900 so far. And yes, I am still annoyed about it. Because I think about how long we would have kept paying that higher rate if that renewal hadn’t finally made me mad enough to check. My neighbor did the same thing after I told him. Clean record, two cars, rate had been creeping up for years. He thought it was just “how insurance is now.” It wasn’t. He found a lower rate in a few minutes. My sister checked hers too. She was bundled and thought that meant she was getting the best deal. She wasn’t. That’s what gets people. They assume being a good customer means they’re being treated like one. But your

Most people don’t think about insurance until it’s too late. One unexpected accident, illness or disaster can wipe you out financially if you’re not prepared. These are the 8 types of insurance I tell everyone to have in place: 1. Term Life Insurance If someone depends on your income, you need life insurance. A 15- to 20-year term policy for 10 to 12 times your income protects your family if something happens to you. 2. Auto Insurance Even one accident can cost thousands. Make sure you’ve got solid liability coverage that protects your wallet as well as your car. 3. Homeowners or Renters Insurance Your home and your stuff need protection. Fires, storms, and break-ins happen more often than you think. 4. Health Insurance A single hospital visit can leave you drowning in bills. Health insurance isn’t optional. It’s protection from one of the biggest threats to your financial future. 5. Long-Term Disability Insurance Your most important asset is your income. If you can’t work because of an illness or injury, disability insurance helps you keep paying the bills. 6. Long-Term Care Insurance Once you hit 60, this becomes essential. Nursing homes and assisted living can cost six figures a year. Don’t let that drain your retirement. 7. Identity Theft Protection Identity theft is everywhere. Good protection means you get a team to clean up the mess and restore your accounts if your info is stolen. 8. Umbrella Insurance This one gives you extra liability coverage beyond your home and auto policies. It’s cheap and worth every penny for the extra protection. Getting this is a good idea for anyone with a net worth of at least $500,000. Don’t wait for a crisis to realize you’re not protected. Get the coverage you need before life throws a curveball: https://ter.li/Coverage_Types
